extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political economy, race/class studies and criminology (researchers studying black labour, unemployment, and policing)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria and distinctions for interpreting the position, composition and political significance of black labour (wageless, reserve army, sub‑proletariat, lumpen) within capitalist/imperialist contexts. Focuses on causes, layers, and political implications of unemployment and marginalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recomposition of capital ('social capital')
rubrics_metrics.description: The recomposition of capital along 'social-capital' lines has been accomplished, principally, by three factors: the reorganisation of the labour process (application of 'Fordist' techniques), the Keynesian revolution in economic management, and the 'integration' of organised institutions of the working class through social democracy and reformism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three factors as explanatory criteria when arguing that capital has become 'social capital' (i.e., the state as 'thinking head' of social capital). Examples: deskilling via Fordist production, post‑war Keynesian full‑employment policies, institutional incorporation of labour via social democratic reforms. Anti-pattern: attributing recomposition to a single cause without reference to labour process, macroeconomic management, and political integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the 'mass worker' (proletarianisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'mass worker' is deskilled, subsumed into massified processes of production, can be moved from one part of a fragmented/automated labour process to another and from one country to another (e.g., migrant labour in advanced capitalist countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accounts of labour by checking for evidence of deskilling, interchangeability of labour across tasks/geographies, and reliance on migrant labour. These features indicate recomposition toward massified, flexible labour. Counter‑evidence would be persistence of craft/skill barriers, localized stable employment, or weak migrant labour presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political recomposition and forms of worker resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Alongside productive recomposition there is a political recomposition: old reflexes and organisations of class struggle are being dismantled and class struggle tends to generate new forms of militant resistance—'organised spontaneity'—often directly at the 'point of production'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing contemporary working‑class struggle, look for localized, spontaneous workplace actions aimed at the new labour process rather than traditional union‑centred tactics. Treat such 'organised spontaneity' as an indicator of political recomposition rather than as mere 'disorder'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wagelessness as ideological versus political strategy (Race Today critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Race Today treats the refusal to work among black labour and black youth as a real phenomenon but argues it represents an ideological, not a fully political, struggle: 'a quasi‑political rebellion, not as a fully formed class perspective'. It does not necessarily 'subvert capital' directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to judge whether wagelessness is being characterized as primarily symbolic/ideological or as a strategic political force. Evidence of widespread, organised political outcomes from refusal to work supports a political reading; isolated cultural/expressive forms support the ideological reading. Beware of reducing wagelessness solely to an economic/reserve‑army effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marx/Engels' lumpenproletariat criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The lumpen proletariat are 'the social scum... the depraved elements of all classes'—parasitic in economic existence, outside productive labour, venal and unreliable as allies for the workers' movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these classic markers when labeling a social grouping as 'lumpen': persistent parasitism, exclusion from productive labour, lack of cohesion or revolutionary tempering by productive experience. Anti-pattern: labelling large, culturally active wageless populations as 'lumpen' without examining their social roles, survival strategies, and political capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of political vibrancy among the wageless (Darcus Howe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Howe describes unemployed/wageless groups as vibrant and powerful: surviving by 'hustling' (not necessarily criminal), producing culture (steel band, calypso, reggae), avoiding humiliation of wage work, developing social discipline through hustling, and able to act as a 'military arm' in political struggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of political potency by seeking evidence of autonomous cultural production, collective organization or disciplined social practices (e.g., gangs negotiated with political leaders), and capacity to influence broader political events (e.g., preventing army intervention). Lack of such evidence suggests a weaker political role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black labour as sub‑proletariat and super‑exploitation (Cambridge / Black Liberator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cambridge and Gutsmore argue the black proletariat is best conceived as a sub‑proletariat: a stratum subject to two mechanisms—super‑exploitation (higher extraction of surplus value) and racial oppression—often structurally below the white working class and frequently forming a disproportionate section of the reserve army of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge analyses of black labour against criteria of double‑oppression: measurable indicators of super‑exploitation (lower pay, worse conditions, higher surplus extraction), racial discrimination, and structural labour market segmentation. Use these to distinguish sub‑proletarian status from purely marginal or lumpen designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve army of labour definition and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: The reserve army exists because capitalism needs a mass of labour always ready for exploitation and the disposability (unemployment) of workers; in imperialist economies, black masses frequently form a substantial section of this industrial reserve army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a group functions as part of the reserve army by examining its disposability (high unemployment/underemployment rates), use as a labour source in expansion phases, and role in disciplining wages/conditions. Empirical indicators: cyclical absorption/expulsion, disproportionate unemployment, and replacement/substitution dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marx's stratification within the reserve army
rubrics_metrics.description: Marx distinguishes strata within the reserve army: floating (repelled/drawn back into production), latent (primarily agricultural displaced into cities), stagnant (irregularly/employed), distinct from lumpenproletariat and pauperism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these finer categories to classify unemployed/marginal groups rather than collapsing them into 'lumpen' or a single undifferentiated reserve. Look for mobility (floating), origins in agriculture (latent), or chronic irregular employment (stagnant) to apply the correct label and analytic expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of size/character of the wageless sector (economic vs political)
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the wageless sector may be governed more by fundamental economic rhythms of capitalist accumulation (Marx's reserve army mechanics) than by a minority's political strategy 'not to take shit‑work any longer'; yet those assigned economically can still develop this into a positive political strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining wagelessness, weigh structural economic causes (accumulation cycles, deskilling, substitution) more heavily but remain open to emergent political agency. Avoid monocausal arguments that ignore either structural economic determinants or possible political transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution, deskilling and recomposition as mechanisms of reserve army formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital composes/recomposes the working class by deskilling and substitution—replacing one sector of labour by a cheaper one—and thereby forming and dissolving the reserve army; these are central processes in the formation/destiny of labour strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess labour market changes for evidence of deskilling (loss of skill requirements), substitution (cheaper/lower‑status labour replacing previous workers), and recomposition (permanent structural shifts). These mechanisms explain shifts in employment status and the creation of disposability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern substitutes for the classical reserve army
rubrics_metrics.description: In post‑war Western Europe, the reserve army in its classical form was difficult to sustain, so modern capitalism used women and migrant labour as substitute 'reserve' sources; migrant workers became a permanent basis of the modern industrial reserve army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contemporary labour regimes by checking for reliance on migrant labour and gendered segmentation as structural substitutes for unemployment‑based reserve armies. Evidence: persistent migrant employment in low‑status jobs, policy regimes facilitating flexible migrant labour, and gendered relegation to precarious roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and characterization in Third World contexts ('underclass'/'subproletariat' vs 'lumpenproletariat')
rubrics_metrics.description: For large urban dispossessed populations in the Third World (shanty‑towns, favelas), the text recommends abandoning the insulting/analytically confusing term 'lumpenproletariat' in favour of 'underclass' or 'subproletariat' because these groups, though often unproductive, are large and economically important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer analytic labels that reflect scale and structural importance (underclass/subproletariat) when describing urban marginal populations in developing countries. Avoid projecting European nineteenth‑century 'lumpen' connotations that obscure the actual economic roles and political potentials of these groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid historicist reduction when explaining present struggles
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat against over‑historicist explanations: do not explain present forms of struggle solely in terms of past traditions or origins; current political factors may recreate opportunities for struggle irrespective of origin history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing the genesis of current political/mobilization forms, balance historical origins with contemporaneous political/economic conditions. Avoid treating present behaviours as mere continuations of past traditions without evidence of causal continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for when wagelessness constitutes a basis for class strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Wagelessness may be a positive, rather than passive, form of struggle when it is a majority (not marginal), culturally and ideologically amplified, and therefore capable of providing the base of a viable class strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether wagelessness can underwrite a class strategy by assessing its numerical scale, degree of cultural/ideological articulation (shared practices, cultural forms), and organisational capacity. If these are substantial, treat wagelessness as a potential strategic base rather than a marginal social problem.
